profile.name: Kaze no bon
profile.tagline: A 300-year-old night festival in Yatsuo where unmarried dancers hide their faces from typhoons.
profile.insight: In the mountain village of Yatsuo, young unmarried dancers hide their faces beneath low-brimmed straw hats to appease the wrath of the wind gods.
profile.profile: Kaze-no-Bon, meaning "Bon Dance of the Wind," is an annual Japanese festival held from September 1 to 3 in Yatsuo, Toyama, Japan. Tracing its history back more than 300 years to the Genroku era, the festival was originally created to appease typhoons and secure a bountiful rice harvest. At night, young unmarried men and women process through the steep, lantern-lit streets of the village, their faces concealed by flat straw hats. Accompanied by the melancholic tones of the kokyū vièle and the traditional shamisen, the dancers move in long parallel files representing the district's eleven quarters.
profile.profile_long:
Kaze-no-Bon, meaning "Bon Dance of the Wind," is a prominent Japanese festival held annually from September 1 to 3 in Yatsuo, a mountain village located in the extended municipality of Toyama on the western coast of Honshu's main island in Japan. The village of Yatsuo, which had 21,810 inhabitants in 2005, extends around three kilometers along the Ida river, nestled between two mountains. The festival takes place in the steep and cobbled streets of the village center, which are illuminated for the occasion by traditional paper lanterns. Having a history of about 300 years, Kaze-no-Bon has existed without interruption since the Genroku era, spanning from 1688 to 1704. Originally, the festival was held in order to appease Shinto divinities and typhoons, allowing for a bountiful harvest of rice during a period when hurricanes and storms are frequent across the Japanese archipelago.

The festival is uniquely held at night, creating an atmosphere that is sometimes described as eerie or mysterious by onlookers, drawing up to 200,000 visitors from across the archipelago. Long rows of young men and women progress slowly in parallel files, dancing simultaneously to a melancholic melody. Each dancing troupe represents one of the eleven districts of the Yatsuo municipal district. Among the performances, the most traditional dance style is the Kyu odori. Another style is the Shin odori, which was introduced later in 1920; in this newer style, the steps of the men and women differ distinctly, with the men's movements evoking the labor of agricultural field work.

The visual presentation of the dancers is defined by precise costuming. The female dancers are dressed in matching cotton kimonos known as yukata and wear flat straw hats called amigasa, which are heavily tilted to conceal their faces. Their male companions wear a short jacket along with a similar straw hat. These hats and matching kimonos cover the dancers' faces to hide them from the wrath of the god they hope to appease, stemming from the fear that the divine anger might otherwise fall upon them. Traditionally, all participating dancers are unmarried, a custom rooted in old ideas that performers might anger the gods and that the performance acts as a form of virginal self-sacrifice. However, modern interpretations also suggest social reasons, such as providing an opportunity for young unmarried people to meet.

At the rear of the night procession, an older female singer leads the traditional village song known as Ecchu Owara Bushi. This vocal line is accompanied by rare and traditional instruments, including the kokyū, a traditional stringed vièle, a traditional shamisen luth with three strings, and drums. This melancholic music is exceptionally unique to the region and was selected in 1996 by the Ministry of the Environment as one of the 100 soundscapes of Japan. In addition to the main street processions, dance groups perform structured demonstrations on stages scattered throughout the village, while private performances are given in local restaurants and private homes. In the middle of the night, once the tourists have departed, the local population of the town joins the dancers in costume, continuing the celebration sometimes until the break of dawn. Beyond the dance itself, the tiny shops lining the village streets offer games, trinkets, traditional foods, and special Japanese paper as popular souvenirs.

sections.origins_and_history: Kaze-no-Bon has a history of about 300 years, existing without interruption since the Genroku era (1688-1704). The original festival was held in order to honor Shinto divinities and appease typhoons so that they would spare the upcoming rice harvest in early September.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Young men and women progress slowly in long parallel files through the streets, dancing simultaneously to a melody. Each troupe represents one of the eleven districts of Yatsuo. The traditional style is Kyu odori, while Shin odori was introduced in 1920, featuring distinct steps for men and women where the men's movements evoke agricultural field work.
sections.music_and_instruments: At the rear of the procession, a well-aged female voice sings Ecchu Owara Bushi, a traditional village song. This voice is accompanied by rare instruments including the kokyū (a traditional stringed vièle), the traditional shamisen (a three-stringed lute), and drums. This music was selected in 1996 by the Ministry of the Environment as one of the 100 soundscapes of Japan.
sections.costume_and_setting: The festival takes place at night in the steep, cobbled center of Yatsuo village, which spans the Ida river between two mountains. The streets are decorated with paper lanterns. Dancers wear matching cotton yukata and flat straw hats called amigasa, which are tilted to cover their faces. Male companions wear a short jacket and a similar hat.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Held annually from September 1 to 3, the festival serves to appease wind and typhoon gods. The dancers hide their faces to protect themselves from the wrath of the gods they hope to appease. Traditionally, performers were strictly unmarried, rooted in ideas of virginal self-sacrifice to avoid angering the deities, though modern interpretations also view it as a chance for young people to meet.
sections.notable_figures: No individual notable figures are named in the source materials.
sections.regional_variants: Each troupe represents one of the eleven districts of the village of Yatsuo, performing dances like the traditional Kyu odori and the later Shin odori.
sections.lineage: Rooted in the Bon Dance tradition and Shinto rituals of the Genroku era.
